title: Scottish Tablet
subtitle: Crystalline Scottish sugar confection
excerpt: A uniquely Scottish confection of sugar, butter, and condensed milk, boiled to the soft ball stage then beaten until it sets into crumbly, intensely sweet, melt-in-the-mouth squares. Harder than fudge, softer than toffee.

recipe.sourceNotes: Scottish tablet is a confection that exists somewhere between fudge and toffee. It is made from sugar, butter, and condensed milk, cooked to the soft ball stage — higher than fudge, which gives it a firmer, more crystalline, crumbly texture that dissolves on the tongue with an intense sweetness. The key stage that distinguishes tablet from fudge is the vigorous beating after the mixture comes off the heat: this breaks down the sugar crystals and causes the mixture to 'grain', turning from a glossy caramel into a pale, matte, grainy paste that sets into the characteristic crystalline texture. The beating must be done immediately the mixture leaves the heat and must be sustained for 5 to 10 minutes. Tablet appears in Scottish records from the early 18th century.

recipeTools.notes: A heavy-based pan, at least 3 litres capacity.
A 20 x 30 cm tin, lined and buttered.

content.text: Use a heavy pan: the mixture will bubble up dramatically at high heat. Stir constantly once the condensed milk goes in or the sugars will catch on the bottom. The mixture is ready at the soft ball stage: 116 to 118 C on a sugar thermometer, or a drop of mixture in cold water forms a soft ball that flattens when squeezed between your fingers. Once off the heat, beat immediately and without stopping until the mixture grains and turns pale and matte. This can take 5 to 10 minutes of vigorous stirring.
Butter a 20 x 30 cm tin and line with baking paper. Dissolve the sugar in the milk and butter in a large, heavy pan over low heat. Stir until no grains remain.

Add the condensed milk. Bring to a boil, stirring constantly. Cook at a rolling boil, stirring constantly and scraping the bottom of the pan, for 20 to 25 minutes until the temperature reaches 116 C on a sugar thermometer, or until a soft ball forms when a drop is placed in cold water.

Remove from the heat immediately. Add the vanilla. Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 5 to 10 minutes until the mixture lightens in colour, turns pale and matte, and thickens noticeably. It will lose its glossy sheen when it is ready.

Pour quickly into the prepared tin, smoothing the top. Score into squares with a sharp knife after 5 minutes, before it fully sets. Leave to cool completely, then break along the score lines into pieces. Keeps in an airtight tin for 2 weeks.
